title: URL Shortener — Class Design
summary: The encoding-scheme trade-off and the encoder/repository class boundary — the class-level version of the HLD scaling question, built around a swappable Encoder abstraction.

slides.markdown:
The HLD version of "design a URL shortener" is about scale: how many redirects per second, how to shard the datastore, how to keep IDs unique across machines. This class-level version is a different, narrower question: what's the actual object model — how does an `Encoder` and a `Repository` divide responsibility so the encoding scheme can change without touching storage, or vice versa.

It's a good intermediate case study precisely because the entities are small, but the one real decision — how to turn a long URL into a short code — has several genuinely different correct answers with different trade-offs.

**In scope:** shortening a long URL into a short code, redirecting a short code back to its long URL, optional custom aliases, and optional per-link expiry.

**Out of scope:** distributed unique-ID generation at scale (multiple machines generating non-colliding IDs concurrently, without a single database bottleneck) — that's the HLD question's job. This class design assumes a single logical ID source and focuses on the object boundaries around encoding and storage.

Being explicit about that boundary is exactly what the interviewer wants to hear: it shows you know this is the class-design half of a two-part problem, not the whole thing.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: UrlMapping, Encoder, Repository, ExpiryPolicy
slides.markdown:
**UrlMapping** is the record: a short code, the original long URL, a creation timestamp, and an optional expiry. **Encoder** is an interface with one real job — turn some input (a counter value, a hash, nothing at all) into a short code string. **Repository** persists and looks up `UrlMapping`s by their short code, with no opinion on how codes are generated. **ExpiryPolicy** decides whether a given `UrlMapping` is still valid.

The interview-relevant design choice is that `Encoder` and `Repository` don't know about each other's internals — a `ShortenerService` composes them, but swapping the encoding scheme never means touching how mappings are stored, and vice versa.

`ShortenerService` depends on the `Encoder` and `Repository` **interfaces**, not on any concrete implementation. A `Base62CounterEncoder` and a `HashEncoder` are two interchangeable `Encoder`s; an in-memory map and a real database are two interchangeable `Repository`s.

This boundary is what makes the encoding-scheme trade-off (next few slides) a real design decision instead of a foregone conclusion baked into the storage layer.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: ShortenerService composes an Encoder and a Repository
The hard part: base62-counter vs hash-with-collisions
slides.markdown:
**Base62 counter**: maintain a global incrementing counter, encode its value in base62 (`[a-zA-Z0-9]`) to get a short code. It's simple and has zero collisions by construction — every counter value is unique — but it needs a single, coordinated counter source, which is exactly the distributed-ID problem the HLD version tackles at scale.

**Hash-of-URL**: hash the long URL (MD5/SHA) and truncate to a few characters. It needs no shared counter and the same URL always maps to the same code, which can be a feature — but truncating a hash means **collisions are possible** (two different URLs truncating to the same short code), so the design needs an explicit collision-handling path, unlike the counter approach.

Neither is "wrong" — the trade-off is coordination-free-but-needs-collision-handling versus collision-free-but-needs-coordination.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: base62 counter vs hash truncation vs random-then-check
slides.markdown:
| | Base62 counter | Hash truncation (MD5/SHA) | Random-then-check |
|---|---|---|
| Collisions possible? | No — every counter value is unique | Yes — different URLs can truncate to the same code | Yes — a random code can already exist |
| Needs coordination? | Yes — one shared counter source | No | No |
| Same URL twice | Produces a new code each time (or needs a lookup-first check) | Produces the same code every time | Produces a new code each time |
| Collision handling needed | None | Required — retry with a longer hash or a salt | Required — retry with a new random code |

**How to decide:** pick the counter when you can afford the coordination cost (or already have the HLD's distributed-ID solution available) for guaranteed uniqueness; pick hash or random when avoiding shared state matters more, and you're willing to add a bounded collision-retry loop.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a bounded collision-retry loop for hash-based encoding
Extending to custom aliases and expiry without changing the contract
slides.markdown:
A custom alias ("shorten this to `/promo2024`") and a per-link expiry both need to slot into the existing `shorten`/`resolve` contract, not replace it. For a custom alias, `ShortenerService` skips calling `Encoder.generate()` entirely and uses the caller-supplied code directly — after checking the `Repository` for a collision, since a human-chosen alias can just as easily already exist as a generated one.

Expiry is even simpler: it's already a field on `UrlMapping`, checked once in `resolve()` (slide 5). Adding expiry never touched `Encoder` or `Repository` at all — it lived entirely in the data model and one `if` in the read path from the start.

Both extensions land without modifying `Encoder` or `Repository`'s interfaces, which is the point of keeping `shorten`/`resolve` as the stable contract everything else builds around.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: exposing the internal counter or ID directly
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Just return the raw counter value (or database auto-increment ID) as the short code — base62-encoding it is an unnecessary extra step."

**Why it's wrong:** it locks the system into exactly one encoding scheme forever, since the short code *is* the internal ID, not a representation of it. It also leaks information — a raw sequential ID tells anyone watching how many URLs have been shortened total, and lets them guess or enumerate other users' links by trying nearby numbers.

**Correct model:** always generate the short code through the `Encoder` abstraction, even for the simplest counter-based scheme. The one extra encode/decode step is what keeps the internal ID private and the encoding scheme swappable later without changing every stored short code's meaning.
